findings.body:
The test asserts the output ends with `…` and is at most 21 bytes, but it never checks *that the cut landed on a word boundary*.  The content of the truncated string is the only thing that proves the `rfind(' ')` logic worked; a bug that cuts exactly at byte 20 (mid-word) would still produce an ellipsis and satisfy `out.len() <= 21`.  Assert that `"Guard the"` is a prefix of the output, or that no word is split, to pin the actual behaviour.

Example of what could regress silently: `shorten` could become `text.chars().take(limit).collect() + "…"` (character-capped but ignoring word boundaries).  Both assertions would pass, but a title like `"Guard the index before"` would become `"Guard the index bef…"` — readable but wrong.

Fix by adding an assertion like:
```rust
        assert!(out.starts_with("Guard the"), "{out}");
```
findings.title: Assert that word-boundary truncation actually stops on a word boundary

findings.body:
The single test passes on `"This is wrong. And here is why."`, which has `. ` (dot-space) as the delimiter.  The branch `text.find(". ")` would *not* match a sentence ending with `.` immediately followed by end-of-string or a newline.  That case (a one-sentence input with no trailing space) is covered by the `None` arm, but the `Some` arm's assumption that `end` points to the `.` before a space is not tested for edge cases like abbreviations (`"e.g. "`) or a terminal period without a following space as in `"Stop. Go."` (note: no space before `"Go"` would still find `. ` because the dot *is* before a space).  The real gap is that the test exercises only one input; add a case where `. ` appears earlier than the true sentence-boundary period (e.g. an abbreviation) to show the limitation is deliberate.

Since this is a new module, coverage is thin; a regression that changes `find(". ")` to `find(".")` would still pass this test.
findings.title: Test that first_sentence extracts only the first sentence when no space follows the dot

value.summary: Introduces embedding config, kernel-bypass entrypoint, and two text-shortening functions.  The two tests in `summarise.rs` cover the main paths of `shorten` and `first_sentence` but both stop assertions short of the behaviour they want to pin: they assert length/trim but not that word-boundary termination or sentence extraction actually happens.  No test exercises the kernel-bypass script, the compose overlays, or the config-mount wiring — but those are infrastructure files whose regression can only be caught by integration tests (none of which changed) and are not silent regressions at the unit level.  The missing assertions on the existing tests tell the author nothing if the code changes shape; they are the real gap.  Everything else looks sound and safe to merge.
